'''Laurence Harris Pearl''' (born 18 June 1956) is a British [[biochemist]] and [[structural biologist]] who is currently Professor of Structural Biology in the Genome Damage and Stability Centre and was Head of the School of [[Life Science]]s at the [[University of Sussex]].<ref name="googlescholar">{{GoogleScholar|oZwWly4AAAAJ}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal

==Education==
Born in Manchester to a working class Jewish family,<ref name="whoswho">{{cite web |url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U246981 |title=PEARL, Prof. Laurence Harris |work=Who's Who 2014, A & C Black, an imprint of Bloomsbury Publishing plc, 2014; online edn, Oxford University Press }}{{subscription required}}</ref> he went to [[Manchester Grammar School]] where he was very active in school drama productions, appearing alongside [[Nicholas Hytner]] in ''[[The Government Inspector]]''. Pearl read Biochemistry at [[University College London]] and then obtained [[Master of Science|MSc]] and PhD degrees in the Department of [[Crystallography]] at [[Birkbeck, University of London|Birkbeck College]], for studies of [[endothiapepsin]] under the supervision of [[Tom Blundell]].<ref name="pearlsphd">{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Laurence|last=Pearl |title=Crystallographic studies of endothiapepsin |publisher=Birkbeck College |year=1984 |url=http://catalogue.ulrls.lon.ac.uk/record=b1528581~S1|author-link=Laurence Pearl}}</ref>
He was part of the [[Birkbeck College]] [[University Challenge]] team who were semi-finalists in 1984, and achieved the 2nd highest score in the show's history - 430 against [[Exeter College, Oxford]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.blanchflower.org/uc/stats_hiscore.html | title=University Challenge - Statistics}}</ref>

==Career==
Following [[Postdoctoral research]] positions at [[Birkbeck, University of London|Birkbeck College]] and the [[Institute of Cancer Research]] in [[Sutton, Surrey]], he returned to UCL as lecturer in Biochemistry in 1989, becoming [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]] and then Professor of Structural Biology in 1996. In 1999 he rejoined the [[Institute of Cancer Research]] to chair the new Section of Structural Biology (jointly with David Barford) at the Chester Beatty Laboratories in [[Chelsea, London|Chelsea]].

In 2009 he was appointed Head of the new School of Life Sciences at the [[University of Sussex]], relocating his laboratory to the [[Medical Research Council (UK)|MRC]] Genome Damage and Stability Centre, where he holds the position of Professor of Structural Biology.

In 2017 he announced that he would be standing down as Head of the School of Life Sciences at Sussex.<ref name="Badge-leavingr">{{cite web | url=http://thebadgeronline.com/2017/05/laurence-pearl-steps-down-life-sciences/ | title=Head of School of Life Sciences steps down | date=31 May 2017 }}</ref>

From October 2017 until June 2026 he held a joint appointment as Head of the Division of Structural Biology at the [[Institute of Cancer Research]] while continuing as Professor of Structural Biology in the [[Genome Damage and Stability Centre]] at the [[University of Sussex]].

==Research and enterprise==

His research focuses on understanding the structural basis for assembly, specificity and regulation of proteins and complexes involved in human diseases such as [[HIV/AIDS]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/images/Drug%20design%20HIV_tcm18-166406.pdf|title = Accredited Degree Programmes}}</ref> and cancer.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/coverstory/85/8509cover.html |title=Chemical & Engineering News: Cover Story - Living on the Edge |access-date=10 October 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080704200547/http://pubs.acs.org/cen/coverstory/85/8509cover.html |archive-date=4 July 2008 |url-status=dead |df=dmy-all }}</ref> He is particularly noted for his early work on the [[HIV-1 protease]], proteins involved in [[DNA repair]] such as [[uracil-DNA glycosylase]] and [[DNA-PKcs]] and the [[Hsp90]]<ref name="hsp90"/> molecular chaperone system. Although focussed on understanding basic mechanisms, his laboratory is committed to translating this understanding to the discovery of new drugs for patient benefit.<ref name="biochemj">{{Cite journal
| pmid = 18290764
| year = 2008
| last1 = Pearl
| first1 = L. H.
| title = The Hsp90 molecular chaperone: An open and shut case for treatment
| journal = Biochemical Journal
| volume = 410
| issue = 3
| pages = 439–53
| last2 = Prodromou
| first2 = C
| last3 = Workman
| first3 = P
| doi = 10.1042/BJ20071640
}}</ref>

He is a founder and CSO of Domainex Ltd,<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.domainex.co.uk/management-team | title=Management Team}}</ref> an innovative biotech company that won the 2010 Life Sciences and Enterprise Programme of The Year Award,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.domainex.co.uk/documents/Domainex-Genesisaward.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=22 October 2011 |archive-date=25 April 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120425083134/http://www.domainex.co.uk/documents/Domainex-Genesisaward.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> and the "Innovation in Enabling Biotechnology" Prize at 2007 UKTI Bioentrepreneurial Company of the Year Awards.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.domainex.co.uk/news2007.asp | title=Press room | access-date=22 October 2011 | archive-date=25 April 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120425083139/http://www.domainex.co.uk/news2007.asp | url-status=dead }}</ref>

On arrival at Sussex he undertook the restructuring of the School of Life Sciences which resulted in nearly one third of the faculty accepting early retirement or leaving the university,<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/story.asp?storycode=409266 | title=Sussex's future: Fewer staff, more students| date=2009-11-27}}</ref> and rationalised the degree programs, stopping a number of poorly-recruiting Masters programmes. Sussex now ranks 8th in the UK in Biosciences in the 2012 Guardian University Guide,<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/table/2011/may/17/university-guide-biosciences | title=University guide 2012: Biosciences| website=[[TheGuardian.com]]| date=2011-05-16}}</ref> and Chemistry, which had been threatened with closure in 2006, has been revitalised with the appointment of new Faculty in Organic and Synthetic Chemistry, and with the launch of a university-funded initiative in Medicinal Chemistry and Drug Discovery.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.sussex.ac.uk/lifesci/drugdiscovery/ | title=Sussex Drug Discovery Centre : University of Sussex}}</ref>

Sussex ranked 10th overall in the UK for Biological Sciences, and 8th for research outputs in the 2014 Research Excellence Framework ([[Research Excellence Framework|REF]]),<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://results.ref.ac.uk/(S(ondfjmjwf3r2idep11x4gw0w))/Results/ByUoa/5 | title=Results & submissions : REF 2014 : View results and submissions by UOA}}</ref> placing it on par with Cambridge and ahead of the majority of Russell Group Universities.

==Awards and honours==

Pearl was elected to membership of the [[European Molecular Biology Organisation|European Molecular Biology Organisation (EMBO)]] in 2005, a Fellow of the [[Academy of Medical Sciences]] (FMedSci) in 2007, a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 2008 and a [[Academia Europaea|Member of the Academia Europaea (MAE)]] in 2012. In 2011 he was awarded an inaugural Senior Investigator Award by the [[Wellcome Trust]].<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.sussex.ac.uk/newsandevents/?id=8265 | title=Wellcome funds 'outstanding' cancer research at Sussex}}</ref> His nomination for the Royal Society reads {{centred pull quote|Laurence Pearl has applied structural, biochemical and genetic techniques, to elucidate the molecular basis of function and specificity in systems of fundamental biomedical importance. His pioneering work on [[retrovirus|retroviral]] [[protease]]s was a key step in the recognition of [[HIV protease]] as a [[Biological target|therapeutic target]] in [[HIV/AIDS|AIDS]]. He has made seminal contributions to our understanding of the recognition and repair of [[DNA repair|DNA damage]]. In studies of the molecular chaperone [[Hsp90]], he was the first to show its function depended on binding and [[hydrolysis]] of [[Adenosine triphosphate|ATP]], and he defined the mechanism of the [[ATPase]]-coupled molecular clamp that drives the chaperone cycle. In his research on cell signalling he has determined the structure of [[GSK-3]]-beta, showing how it recognises substates, and elucidating how it is inhibited through [[insulin]] signalling.<ref name="royal"/>}}

Pearl and his research team were awarded the 2013 [[Cancer Research UK]] Translational Cancer Research Prize<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.cancerresearchuk.org/cancer-info/news/archive/pressrelease/2013-11-05-research-prize-winners-announced |title=Archived copy |access-date=10 November 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131110092555/http://www.cancerresearchuk.org/cancer-info/news/archive/pressrelease/2013-11-05-research-prize-winners-announced |archive-date=10 November 2013 |url-status=dead |df=dmy-all }}</ref> along with the team of [[Paul Workman (scientist)|Paul Workman]] at the [[Institute of Cancer Research]] for their seminal work in developing the [[Hsp90]] [[molecular chaperone]] as a new target for cancer therapy and for their role in development of the drug [[AUY922]].

Laurence Pearl was awarded the 2018 Novartis Medal and Prize<ref name="biochemistry.org">{{Cite web|url=http://www.biochemistry.org/Awards/2018Winners.aspx|title=2018 Award Winners &#124; Biochemistry|date=17 May 2019|access-date=11 April 2017|archive-date=12 April 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170412063025/http://www.biochemistry.org/Awards/2018Winners.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.biochemistry.org/Awards/TheNovartisMedalandPrize.aspx | title=The Novartis Medal and Prize &#124; Biochemical Society | access-date=11 April 2017 | archive-date=7 June 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170607233600/http://www.biochemistry.org/Awards/TheNovartisMedalandPrize.aspx | url-status=dead }}</ref> from the [[Biochemical Society]] for his significant contributions to our understanding of the biochemical and structural basis for assembly, specificity and regulation of the proteins and complexes that carry out DNA repair and DNA damage signalling, signal transduction, and chaperone-dependent protein activation.
